clue.text: We dramatically slaughtered a wealthy spinster

indicators.note: slaughtered says the letters of the words before it are hacked apart and put together again in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written as part of the fodder

explanation.surface: A theatrical confession that the speakers did away with a rich unmarried woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is WE DRAMATICALLY, fourteen letters that 'slaughtered' rearranges into the name. She is Miss Crawley, the rich aunt courted for her money in Thackeray's Vanity Fair.
explanation.definitionFit: In Vanity Fair the old maid Miss Crawley is courted by relatives hoping to inherit her large fortune.

clue.text: A work including sound that's continuous

parts.note: to go is to work or function, as a machine does
a tone is a musical sound

explanation.surface: A piece of music that has a sustained note running through it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in a single uninterrupted attempt is continuous, with no break.

clue.text: London is important in this fruity tale, set somewhere dodgy in the southeast

definitions.text: London is important in this fruity tale

parts.note: taken as written
dodgy means doubtful or dubious
Battle is a town in East Sussex, in the south-east of England, site of the 1066 battle

explanation.surface: A tale of fruit set in a shady corner of south-east England in which the capital plays a big part.
explanation.walkthrough: London is not the city but the strike leader in Steinbeck's novel about striking Californian apple pickers. The novel is set, punningly, 'in dubious Battle', the East Sussex town (in the southeast) made doubtful.
explanation.definitionFit: Steinbeck's novel follows a strike among fruit pickers, with the organiser named London a central figure.

explanation.surface: A rueful thought about some little thing the speaker will never own.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny round mark is something small, and the capital I standing for a person is written without one.

clue.text: Announce film about central East Timor? That's obscure

explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic remark is mysterious or obscure, hiding its meaning.

clue.text: Joyce Carey's experience of horror fiction readers

definitions.text: Joyce Carey's experience of horror fiction readers

parts.words: Joyce Carey's experience of horror fiction readers

explanation.surface: What the novelist knew about the thrill people get from reading horror.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist's name is usually spelt Joyce Cary; his 1952 novel's title doubles as a description of the delight in being frightened.
explanation.definitionFit: Readers of horror enjoy being scared, a pleasure mixed with dread, which is also the title of a Cary novel.

clue.text: If this poem is a D clue, Theo Dell might provide the answer

parts.note: read the poem's title as wordplay: love is O, the valley is THE DELL, and putting O in it spells the name Theo Dell

explanation.surface: A setter explaining that a man called Theo Dell could crack a clue to a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the title, taken as a cryptic instruction, puts O (love, a zero score in tennis) inside THE DELL to make THEODELL. 'D clue' suggests a down clue, which this is. The poem is George Meredith's.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's well-known poem has this title, so 'this poem' points at the work itself.

clue.text: A police force that's succeeded, identifying criminals

parts.note: the Yard is Scotland Yard, the London Metropolitan Police
i.e., short for id est, means that is
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies

explanation.surface: Someone says a constabulary that has got results is naming offenders.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Jamaican-origin gangs are called by this name, so the answer is a kind of criminal.

clue.text: A character with a reputation for depravity rested only on corruption

definitions.text: A character with a reputation for depravity

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notorious for vice built his good name on nothing but dishonesty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corruption' sounds like part of the moral picture but is the anagram signal, turning RESTED ONLY into the wicked peer of Thackeray's Vanity Fair.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marquis of Steyne in Vanity Fair is a dissolute aristocrat known for vice.

clue.text: Stanhope's driver, always content

indicators.note: content means what is held inside, so the answer sits within the words driver, always

explanation.surface: A remark that Stanhope's chauffeur is never anything but satisfied.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a first name: Vera Stanhope is the gruff Northumberland detective of Ann Cleeves's novels and the ITV series. 'Content' looks like 'happy' but means the contents.
explanation.definitionFit: DCI Stanhope in Ann Cleeves's crime novels has this first name, so it is what belongs to Stanhope.

clue.text: We met bishops and a social reformer

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: We had an encounter with some clergy and a campaigner for change.
explanation.walkthrough: Sidney and Beatrice Webb were Fabian socialists who founded the London School of Economics.
explanation.definitionFit: Beatrice and Sidney Webb campaigned for welfare and labour reform in Britain.

clue.text: Work with religious message from controversial radical feminist, one interrupting an event in Siena

parts.note: the Palio is the famous bareback horse race run in Siena's main square
TERF stands for trans-exclusionary radical feminist, a contested label
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A religious work from a divisive feminist that disrupts a festival in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Palio is Siena's bareback horse race around the Piazza del Campo; TERF is a contested label, which is why the clue calls the feminist controversial.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece with a devotional theme is a work carrying a religious message.

clue.text: Many have translated this precis — I do so poorly

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A self-deprecating translator admits to summarising a much-translated work badly.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Horace's ode beginning 'Persicos odi, puer, apparatus', translated by countless English poets.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace's short ode is among the most often rendered into English, so many hands have translated it.

clue.text: Sees and hears stories from a Yorkshire poet

explanation.walkthrough: Ken Smith (1938-2003) was a poet born in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken Smith was an English poet from East Yorkshire, author of The Poet Reclining.

clue.text: Number one fan of a key transportation inventor in a sci fi movie

Elisha Otis invented the safety elevator

explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' looks like a job but is the insect. Miss Crawley in Vanity Fair is the aunt everyone courts.

definitions.text: far off on the Heights of Abraham?
definitions.meaning: General Wolfe's men at Quebec would see distant country past the heights

explanation.surface: A general's unfinished business, and the distant view from the battlefield at Quebec.
explanation.walkthrough: Two Wolfes: the American novelist Thomas Wolfe and General James Wolfe, who died taking Quebec on the Heights of Abraham in 1759.
